clues: Around 3000-2500BCE, this was described in the Edwin Smith Papyrus, an ancient Egyptian medical text, where several cases were mentioned as an incurable condition, suggesting treatment via cauterization with a tool called the 'fire drill'. Other historical treatments included bloodletting or even placing raw veal on ulcerated tissue based on the belief that it would feed internal 'worms' devouring the flesh.

Historically, this was sometimes called the 'nun's disease' because it was observed to affected nuns at higher rates than other populations. It was later confirmed that lifelong celibacy increases the risk of this disease.
In the 1990s, the pink ribbon became a global symbol for awareness and advocacy for this disease, sparking public education and leaps in research funding

In 1947, the 'Four Brothers' was a famous jazz tune that became a jazz standard featuring three tenor saxophones and one baritone saxophone. Unfortunately, all four saxophonists who played in the original lineup later developed this disease, which was common amongst jazz musicians at that time.

The name of this condition was coined in 1819 by Rene Laennec, who is more famously known for inventing the stethoscope. He derived it from the Greek word meaning 'orange-yellow' describing the color of the diseased organ

During the American Prohibition, mortality rates of this disease dropped by more than 50%. In modern times, viral causes remain common in many parts of the world although incidence in the Americas is dropping with an increase in metabolic and alcohol related cases.

This medication is sometimes described as 'promiscuous' as it binds to many targets to cause cell death. Iron-mediated cleavage forms reactive carbon radicals that bind to and destroy vital proteins and cell membranes.

In the late 1960s, soldiers in the Vietnam War suffered greatly from drug-resistant malaria. The Vietnamese army asked China for help and the Chinese government started a classified military operation to find a new cure. Tu Youyou found a 4th century text that recommended soaking sweet wormwood in cold water to treat intermittent fevers which led to the discovery of this medication
This medication remains part of the global standard first-line treatment for malaria in ACTs. It is the 'A' in that acronym.

George Gulliver was the first to describe these in 1842, reffering to them as 'spherules' although he did not fully understand their function. Giulio Bizzozero is widely credited as the true discoverer of these in 1881.
These are actually just pieces of cytoplasm broken off from giant cells and do not have DNA or a nucleus.

Only about 20% the size of a red blood cell, your body makes about 100 billion of these each day. Normally, these are disc shaped, but at a site of injury, they grow long, spider-like tentacles (filopodia) to grab onto the dammaged area and other blood cells to form a seal.
In the 18th century, farmers noted some sheep developed pruritis and compulsively scratched their hides against fixed objects, a disease now known as scrapie which is caused by this.
This infectious agent contains no genetic material. It can survive standard sterilization methods including extreme heat, radiation, and formaldehyde.
Multiple diseases are caused by this misfolded protein including Creutzfeldt-Jakob, Kuru, and Bovine spongiform encephalopathy or mad cow disease
